subtopic_detail: Escalation of respiratory support in an infant with bronchiolitis on general paediatric ward
stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the general ward at 2 am. A 4 month old term infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day history of coryza, cough and increasing work of breathing. His mother says he took only 30 percent of his usual feeds today and has had 2 wet nappies in 24 hours. His weight is 6.4 kg and he is fully immunised.

On examination he is alert but tachypnoeic with moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze and fine crackles. His nappy is dry. Nasopharyngeal aspirate is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Feeding: 30% of baseline oral intake in past 12 hours, 2 wet nappies in 24 hours
data_table.Chest: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, no tracheal tug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate respiratory intervention?

options.text: Start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min via a humidified circuit, titrate to keep SpO2 at or above 90 percent, and reassess work of breathing in one hour
options.rationale: Bronchiolitis with SpO2 below 90 percent and moderate work of breathing needs low flow nasal oxygen first line, titrated to a target SpO2 of at least 90 percent. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Start high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min via humidified circuit and admit to the high dependency unit for close monitoring now
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail a trial of low flow oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min after at least 1 to 2 hours; it is not the first respiratory step in ward level bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, and repeat if the work of breathing persists
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol and adrenaline are not recommended in viral bronchiolitis under 12 months; they do not change length of stay or oxygen requirement. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, review in one hour, and start oxygen only if the SpO2 drops further overnight
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in acute viral bronchiolitis; delaying oxygen when SpO2 is already 89 percent is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now with pressure support because his respiratory rate and recession predict imminent respiratory failure requiring definitive airway
options.rationale: He is alert with only moderate recession and no apnoea; escalation should begin with the least invasive effective option, which is low flow oxygen. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: Bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months is managed supportively with feeding support and oxygen. Low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min is the first line respiratory support, titrated to SpO2 of at least 90 percent. High flow nasal cannula is a second line intervention for infants failing low flow after 1 to 2 hours, not a first choice. Bronchodilators, adrenaline, corticosteroids and antibiotics have no routine role.
key_points: Low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min is first line; target SpO2 at or above 90 percent.
High flow nasal cannula is second line after failure of low flow.
Bronchodilators, nebulised adrenaline and corticosteroids do not change outcomes in viral bronchiolitis.
explanation.pearls: SpO2 target in bronchiolitis is 90 percent on room air; start low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min and reassess before escalating to high flow.

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid selection and disposition in moderate viral croup in an emergency department
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 22 month old girl is brought in at midnight with a 12 hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing that started after a 2 day coryzal illness. She is settled on her mother's lap and pink. She has stridor audible only when she becomes upset and moderate intercostal recession at rest. Her chest is otherwise clear.

She has no drooling, no toxic appearance and no history of intubation, asthma or immunodeficiency. She is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degC
data_table.Airway: Barking cough, hoarse voice, stridor only on agitation, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Work of breathing: Moderate intercostal recession at rest, no tracheal tug, no fatigue

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 now, and admit to a monitored bed for at least 4 hours
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg dexamethasone plus nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup with stridor at rest and marked recession or exhaustion, not moderate croup that settles when calm. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe in the emergency short stay area for 4 hours before deciding disposition
options.rationale: Moderate croup is treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; observation for a few hours is appropriate if there was no nebulised adrenaline. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days at home, arrange general practice review the following morning and discharge the child now
options.rationale: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg is an alternative if dexamethasone is not available, but a single dose is used, not a 3 day course; observation before discharge is still required. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give humidified air by face mask alone and reassess in one hour, avoiding any corticosteroid because of the risk of secondary bacterial tracheitis
options.rationale: Humidified air alone does not improve viral croup and there is no evidence that dexamethasone increases bacterial tracheitis; steroid is standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg immediately and arrange urgent ear nose and throat review for consideration of nasoendoscopy to exclude epiglottitis
options.rationale: There is no drooling, tripod posture or toxic appearance; empirical ceftriaxone and nasoendoscopy are not indicated for classic viral croup. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: Viral croup severity is graded by stridor and recession at rest. Mild and moderate croup are both treated with a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. The higher dose of 0.6 mg/kg with nebulised adrenaline is reserved for severe croup, defined by stridor and marked recession at rest with agitation or exhaustion. Observation for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline is required before discharge; a shorter period is acceptable after oral steroid alone.
key_points: Mild or moderate croup: single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg.
Severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000.
Observe for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline before considering discharge.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only on agitation with moderate recession is moderate croup: give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and observe for a few hours before discharge.

subtopic_detail: Investigation of a febrile well appearing infant under three months in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 5 week old boy is brought in by his parents because of a rectal temperature of 38.4 degC at home an hour ago. He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery, is exclusively breast fed and has been feeding normally. He looks pink, alert and content in his father's arms in the cubicle. He has no rash, no bulging fontanelle and no focal signs of infection.

His mother had negative group B streptococcus screening in pregnancy. He has had no contact with anyone with known infection and has not travelled overseas. He is not on any medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 76/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.2 degC
data_table.General: Alert, well perfused, no rash, anterior fontanelle soft and flat
data_table.Focus of infection: Ears, throat and skin unremarkable; no cough, no vomiting, no diarrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, give paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally and discharge home with advice to return if the fever exceeds 39 degC or the infant becomes unwell
options.rationale: Well appearance in an infant under 3 months does not exclude serious bacterial infection; discharging without workup is unsafe at this age. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take a bag urine specimen only, discharge home once the sample is sent and arrange telephone follow up with the general practitioner in 24 hours
options.rationale: Under 3 months of age with fever, the required investigations include blood culture and lumbar puncture as well as urine; bag urine is unreliable and cannot be sent as the only investigation. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Full septic screen including blood culture, urine catheter specimen, lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin now
options.rationale: A rectal temperature of 38 degC or higher in an infant less than 3 months is a full septic workup indication irrespective of appearance, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Take blood cultures and inflammatory markers only and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily, deferring lumbar puncture until results are back
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture should not be deferred pending markers in an infant less than 6 weeks with fever unless there is a contraindication; ceftriaxone monotherapy is also not the preferred neonatal regimen. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

options.text: Admit for 48 hours of observation without any investigations or antibiotics, and perform investigations only if the fever recurs above 38 degC on the ward
options.rationale: Watchful waiting without investigation in an infant under 3 months with documented fever is unsafe and misses early treatable bacterial infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile Child)

explanation.summary: Any infant less than 3 months old with a documented temperature of at least 38 degC needs a full septic workup regardless of general appearance because the risk of serious bacterial infection is high and clinical assessment is unreliable at this age. Investigations include blood culture, urine by catheter or suprapubic aspirate and lumbar puncture, with empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin in Australia. Bag urine is not sent as a definitive specimen. Watching without investigation is unsafe.
key_points: Infant under 3 months with fever at or above 38 degC: full septic workup regardless of appearance.
Catheter or suprapubic urine, blood culture and lumbar puncture are all needed.
Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is the standard neonatal regimen.
explanation.pearls: A well looking infant under 3 months with fever still needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin; do not send bag urine alone or defer the lumbar puncture.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in Neonates

subtopic_detail: First hour management of severe acute asthma in a school aged child in emergency
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar. A 6 year old girl is brought in by ambulance with a 12 hour history of worsening wheeze and cough after a viral upper respiratory illness. She is on inhaled salbutamol as needed and fluticasone 100 mcg twice daily. She has needed her reliever every hour at home overnight.

On arrival she is anxious, sits forwards and can only speak in single words. She has widespread wheeze with markedly reduced air entry at the bases, subcostal and tracheal tug and moderate use of accessory muscles. She is not obviously exhausted and there is no cyanosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 /min, SpO2 89% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Respiratory: Widespread wheeze, reduced air entry at bases, subcostal and tracheal tug, single word sentences
data_table.Peak flow: Unable to perform because of dyspnoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first hour management?

options.text: Give intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 mcg/kg/min immediately as a bolus and continuous infusion in preference to inhaled bronchodilator via spacer therapy
options.rationale: Intravenous salbutamol is reserved for life threatening asthma failing inhaled therapy; inhaled salbutamol via spacer is first line even in severe cases. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg immediately as first line therapy and start non invasive ventilation while awaiting paediatric intensive care review
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is second line, reserved for severe or life threatening asthma not responding to initial salbutamol, prednisolone and ipratropium in the first hour. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give a single dose of nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000, oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once and start empirical amoxicillin for likely bacterial pneumonia today
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is not first line in asthma; dexamethasone is not the preferred oral corticosteroid; empirical antibiotics are not indicated for asthma exacerbations without pneumonia. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give salbutamol 12 puffs via metered dose inhaler and spacer every 20 minutes for one hour, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent
options.rationale: In severe childhood asthma, first hour treatment is back to back salbutamol via spacer (or nebulised if unable), oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg and titrated oxygen; ipratropium is added if response is poor. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

options.text: Give inhaled fluticasone 500 mcg via spacer every hour and defer systemic corticosteroid until the child has failed 4 hours of inhaled controller escalation
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are not effective for acute exacerbations; systemic corticosteroid is given in the first hour to reduce admission and relapse. (Source: RCH CPG: Asthma Acute)

explanation.summary: Severe acute asthma in a child needs immediate salbutamol delivered by spacer (12 puffs for over 6 years) every 20 minutes for the first hour, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg or intravenous methylprednisolone if oral not tolerated) and titrated oxygen to SpO2 above 94 percent. Ipratropium 8 puffs is added by spacer if the response is inadequate. Second line therapy is intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes for life threatening or non responding exacerbations, then intravenous salbutamol or aminophylline. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is pneumonia.
key_points: First hour: 12 puffs salbutamol via spacer every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen.
Add ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer if inadequate response in the first hour.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg is second line for severe or non responding cases.
explanation.pearls: Severe childhood asthma first hour: back to back inhaled salbutamol 12 puffs every 20 minutes, oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg, titrated oxygen and add ipratropium for poor response.

subtopic_detail: Choice of reduction versus surgical exploration in confirmed ileocolic intussusception with equivocal peritonism
stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar on call. A 9 month old boy presents with 8 hours of episodes where he suddenly draws his knees up and cries, settles between episodes but has become progressively more lethargic. He has vomited twice, once was bile stained. He has passed a small amount of blood stained mucus in his nappy.

He is pale and quiet. His abdomen is soft with a long thin lump felt in the right upper part of his tummy on his mother's report; on your examination there is mild fullness in the right upper quadrant but no rigidity. He has capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Ultrasound in the emergency department shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant with preserved perfusion on Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.5 degC
data_table.Abdomen: Soft, mild right upper quadrant fullness, no guarding, no peritonism, no palpable mass on your examination
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound target sign right upper quadrant, preserved mesenteric perfusion on Doppler, no free fluid, no pneumatosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give a barium enema without pre procedure fluid resuscitation, cross match or antibiotic cover so that the intervention can happen immediately without any delay
options.rationale: Barium is not used in AU centres because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs; pre procedure resuscitation and cross match are standard. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Take him directly to theatre for open laparotomy and manual reduction now, bypassing enema attempt because bile stained vomiting predicts perforation and enema failure
options.rationale: Bile stained vomiting alone is not a contraindication to air enema; without peritonism, perforation or shock, enema reduction is attempted first with surgical backup. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Give a nasogastric bolus of polyethylene glycol solution, admit for observation for spontaneous reduction and repeat ultrasound in 4 hours before further steps
options.rationale: Osmotic laxatives are not used to reduce intussusception; observation alone risks progression to ischaemia and perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Give intravenous ondansetron and paracetamol and discharge home once the vomiting settles because the abdomen is not tender and the child looks stable
options.rationale: Confirmed intussusception on ultrasound requires urgent reduction and admission; discharge home is unsafe. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

options.text: Resuscitate with intravenous crystalloid, cross match blood, give intravenous antibiotics and proceed to air enema reduction in the interventional radiology suite
options.rationale: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism, perforation or shock is managed by air enema reduction after resuscitation, cross match and antibiotic cover, with surgery on standby. (Source: RCH CPG: Intussusception)

explanation.summary: Ileocolic intussusception in infants presents with paroxysmal crying, drawing up the legs, vomiting and blood stained mucus in the nappy. Ultrasound target sign is diagnostic. Provided there is no peritonism, perforation on imaging, or refractory shock, first line treatment in Australia is air (pneumatic) enema reduction in interventional radiology after intravenous fluid resuscitation, blood cross match and antibiotic cover, with paediatric surgery on standby. Barium is avoided because of chemical peritonitis risk if perforation occurs. Surgery is reserved for peritonism, perforation, failed enema or a lead point.
key_points: Diagnosis by ultrasound target sign; look for signs of ischaemia and perforation before deciding.
Air enema is first line if no peritonism, perforation or refractory shock; resuscitate and give antibiotics first.
Surgery indications: peritonism, perforation, failed enema reduction or identified lead point.
explanation.pearls: Ileocolic intussusception without peritonism goes to air enema reduction after fluids, cross match and antibiotics; barium is not used because of chemical peritonitis risk.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Journal of Surgery Intussusception Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Choosing intensive phototherapy versus exchange transfusion in a term neonate with rising bilirubin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on the postnatal ward. A term boy weighing 3.4 kg was born by normal vaginal delivery 60 hours ago. His mother is A rhesus positive and he is O rhesus positive. He was noticed to look yellow by the midwife at 48 hours and started single surface phototherapy 8 hours ago. His serum bilirubin at that time was 380 micromol/L.

He is alert with a strong cry, feeding well and passing urine and meconium. He has no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly and no signs of encephalopathy. Repeat total serum bilirubin now, on treatment, is 405 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. Haemoglobin is 145 g/L (145 to 225).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 42 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Bilirubin trend: Total serum bilirubin 380 micromol/L at 52 h, 405 micromol/L at 60 h on single surface phototherapy
data_table.Laboratory: Haemoglobin 145 g/L (145 to 225), direct antiglobulin test positive, no reticulocyte data yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to exchange transfusion now because the bilirubin is rising despite phototherapy and the direct antiglobulin test is positive, without escalating to intensive phototherapy first
options.rationale: Intensive multiple surface phototherapy is escalated first; exchange is reserved for failure to respond, or bilirubin above the exchange line, or acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Escalate to intensive multiple surface phototherapy, ensure adequate feeding and hydration, repeat serum bilirubin in 4 hours and cross match blood for possible exchange
options.rationale: Bilirubin rising above the phototherapy line with a positive direct antiglobulin test in a haemolytic pattern needs intensive phototherapy and blood cross match while awaiting the response; exchange is not yet mandatory. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Stop phototherapy for 6 hours to allow oral feeding and rebound assessment, and repeat serum bilirubin off treatment before deciding on further phototherapy
options.rationale: Stopping phototherapy in a haemolytic pattern with rising bilirubin above threshold risks progression to acute bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg over 4 hours as first line and defer any further phototherapy escalation to allow this treatment to take effect first
options.rationale: Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered in rhesus or ABO haemolytic disease not responding to intensive phototherapy, not before intensive phototherapy has been tried. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

options.text: Continue single surface phototherapy at the current settings, offer formula top ups every 3 hours and repeat serum bilirubin in 12 hours to reassess trajectory
options.rationale: Single surface phototherapy has already failed to control the rise; delaying escalation for 12 hours risks bilirubin encephalopathy. (Source: NSW Health Neonatal Jaundice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Neonatal jaundice management is guided by hour specific bilirubin nomograms with separate phototherapy and exchange transfusion thresholds and by risk factors including haemolytic pattern, prematurity and clinical instability. A positive direct antiglobulin test suggests ABO or rhesus haemolysis and lowers the treatment threshold. When bilirubin rises despite single surface phototherapy, the next step is intensive multiple surface phototherapy plus attention to hydration and feeding, with blood cross match in preparation for exchange. Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered if intensive phototherapy fails in immune haemolytic disease. Exchange transfusion is indicated when bilirubin exceeds the exchange line or acute bilirubin encephalopathy develops.
key_points: Escalate to intensive phototherapy before considering exchange when bilirubin rises above threshold.
Positive direct antiglobulin test lowers thresholds and warrants cross match early.
Intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg is second line after intensive phototherapy in immune haemolysis.
explanation.pearls: Rising serum bilirubin above threshold on single phototherapy with positive direct antiglobulin test: escalate to intensive multiple surface phototherapy, cross match blood and consider intravenous immunoglobulin before exchange.

subtopic_detail: Secondary prophylaxis regimen in a first episode of acute rheumatic fever without carditis in a high risk community
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 11 year old girl from a remote Northern Territory community in a paediatric outpatient clinic. She had a first episode of acute rheumatic fever 6 weeks ago meeting the 2020 Australian guideline criteria: polyarthritis and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with a positive antistreptolysin O titre. Her transthoracic echocardiogram at the time and today shows no valvular abnormality. She has no allergies and is otherwise well.

Her family lives in a household of 9 people with intermittent running water. She has previously missed clinic appointments because of travel time. She is Aboriginal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Cardiac: Dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no signs of heart failure, echocardiogram without valve abnormality now and at index episode
data_table.Social: Remote community, household of 9, intermittent running water, previous missed appointments

lead_in: What is the most appropriate secondary prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once weekly for 3 years and repeat echocardiogram at that point to decide whether to continue prophylaxis at all after treatment
options.rationale: Azithromycin is not the preferred agent in AU; duration is not 3 years and echocardiography is not used to decide when to stop. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily for 5 years, provided adherence is checked at each clinic visit, and stop at that point regardless of episode number
options.rationale: Oral penicillin is second line only if intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin cannot be given; a 5 year fixed duration is not the AU standard. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscular every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer, delivered through the local clinic
options.rationale: In Australia, secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever without carditis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer, especially in a high risk community. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: No secondary prophylaxis because carditis is absent, and use aspirin 60 mg/kg/day only if symptoms of arthritis recur during the following clinic year
options.rationale: Absence of carditis does not remove the need for prophylaxis; recurrent episodes are common and cause carditis on subsequent presentations. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units intramuscular every 12 weeks and short course prednisolone 1 mg/kg for one month, then review need at annual clinic review
options.rationale: The correct dosing interval is 28 days (or 21 days in special situations), not 12 weeks; prednisolone is not used for prevention. (Source: RHDAustralia 2020 Guideline)

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis after acute rheumatic fever prevents recurrent group A streptococcal infection and progression to rheumatic heart disease. In Australia the first line agent is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days. Duration is stratified by the episode and outcome: at least 10 years after the last episode or until age 21 (whichever is longer) for acute rheumatic fever without carditis; longer in the presence of persistent or worsening rheumatic heart disease. Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is reserved for patients who cannot receive intramuscular therapy. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from high risk communities have a high recurrence risk that justifies the longer duration.
key_points: First line: intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days.
Duration for acute rheumatic fever without carditis: at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin twice daily is second line for those unable to have intramuscular therapy.
explanation.pearls: Australian secondary prophylaxis for acute rheumatic fever is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.2 million units every 28 days for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer; longer if carditis or rheumatic heart disease is present.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Acute Rheumatic Fever

subtopic_detail: Emergency management of suspected cerebral oedema during treatment for paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis with borderline neurology
stem:
You are the paediatric intensive care registrar. A 9 year old boy weighing 30 kg has been on the DKA pathway for 4 hours after presenting with a first diagnosis of type 1 diabetes. His initial venous pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L and blood glucose 32 mmol/L. He has received a 10 mL/kg saline bolus and is on maintenance plus deficit fluids at the 5 percent dehydration rate with a fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour.

Over the last 30 minutes his mother reports he has become slower to answer and has complained of a new headache. His Glasgow Coma Score has fallen from 15 to 13 (E4 V4 M5). His pulse has fallen from 128 to 88 with blood pressure rising from 106/62 to 138/78. He has no seizures. There is no focal neurology and the pupils are equal and reactive. Blood glucose is now 12 mmol/L and venous pH is 7.18.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Score 13 (E4 V4 M5), new headache, pupils 3 mm equal and reactive, no focal signs, no seizure
data_table.Biochemistry: Blood glucose 12 mmol/L, venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, arrange urgent contrast CT brain before any osmotherapy and delay retrieval until imaging is complete for the boy
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is not first line for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA; imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline immediately for suspected hypovolaemic shock, then increase the maintenance fluid rate to 1.5 times maintenance for the next hour
options.rationale: The clinical picture is Cushing response with intracranial hypertension, not hypovolaemia; further crystalloid bolus and higher rates worsen cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and add intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the residual acidosis and reduce the ketone load faster
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is a recognised risk factor for cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA and is not recommended; higher insulin does not treat cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give hypertonic 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg intravenously over 15 minutes, reduce the fluid rate by a third, nurse head up 30 degrees and call the retrieval service now
options.rationale: Falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache and rising blood pressure with bradycardia meet AU paediatric DKA criteria for cerebral oedema; hypertonic saline (or 20 percent mannitol), fluid reduction and neurosurgical retrieval are first line. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

options.text: Continue current fluids unchanged, give oral paracetamol 15 mg/kg for the headache and reassess Glasgow Coma Score every 15 minutes over the next hour of observation
options.rationale: Observation without acting on falling Glasgow Coma Score and Cushing response allows brainstem herniation; osmotherapy must not be delayed. (Source: APEG DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of death in paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis and often develops during the first 4 to 12 hours of treatment. Diagnostic clues include a falling Glasgow Coma Score, new headache, incontinence, bradycardia with rising blood pressure (Cushing response) and cranial nerve palsies. Australian paediatric guidelines require immediate osmotherapy with 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes or 20 percent mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg, reduction of intravenous fluid rate by around a third, head up positioning and urgent neurosurgical retrieval. Bicarbonate, further fluid boluses and rapid glucose falls are risk factors and should be avoided. Imaging must not delay osmotherapy when clinical criteria are met.
key_points: Cushing response and falling Glasgow Coma Score in DKA meet clinical criteria for cerebral oedema.
Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 2 to 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg immediately and reduce fluid rate.
Bicarbonate use, aggressive volume and rapid glucose fall are recognised risk factors.
explanation.pearls: New headache with falling Glasgow Coma Score and bradycardia and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment is cerebral oedema: give hypertonic 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg immediately, cut the fluid rate by a third and call retrieval.

sources.label: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines: DKA and Hyperglycaemic Hyperosmolar State

subtopic_detail: Third line uterotonic choice for atonic postpartum haemorrhage after first line failure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 32 year old G3 P2 woman has just delivered a healthy 3900 g baby by uncomplicated vaginal birth after a spontaneous labour. Active management of the third stage was performed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units at the anterior shoulder. Ten minutes after placental delivery she has ongoing brisk vaginal bleeding estimated at 1200 mL. The placenta appears complete on inspection.

Her past history includes essential hypertension well controlled on amlodipine and a healthy body mass index of 26. She has no bronchospastic disease. Her uterus is felt to be poorly contracted and her fundus is at 2 cm above the umbilicus. An intravenous oxytocin bolus of 5 units has been given and an infusion of 40 units in 1 L Hartmann solution is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Uterus: Poorly contracted, fundus 2 cm above umbilicus, ongoing brisk bleeding after oxytocin bolus and infusion
data_table.Genital tract: Placenta complete on inspection, no cervical or vaginal laceration identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Bilateral uterine artery embolisation now before any further uterotonic escalation because pharmacological options in AU practice have already failed her
options.rationale: Embolisation is a later step for ongoing bleeding after failed medical and mechanical therapies; ergometrine, tranexamic acid and mechanical measures come first. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg before ergometrine because it works faster and can be repeated every 15 minutes to a total dose of 2 mg to arrest bleeding
options.rationale: Carboprost is a third line uterotonic in AU practice, used if ergometrine is contraindicated or ineffective, not before ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular misoprostol 800 mcg rectally alone without ergometrine because it has fewer contraindications than the injectable ergot alkaloid agents
options.rationale: Misoprostol is considered when ergometrine is contraindicated and injectable options are unavailable; it is not the preferred second line agent when oxytocin fails. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes to promote uterine relaxation and improve placental site healing before further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate causes uterine relaxation and would worsen atony; it is not a treatment for PPH. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg after checking that there is no contraindication and giving intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g as an adjunct
options.rationale: In atonic PPH after oxytocin, ergometrine is the second line uterotonic if not contraindicated, and tranexamic acid 1 g is given within 3 hours. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian escalation for atonic postpartum haemorrhage is oxytocin (5 units intravenous bolus then 40 units in 1 L Hartmann infusion), then ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular or slow intravenous if there is no contraindication (hypertension, pre-eclampsia, cardiac disease), then carboprost 250 mcg intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 2 mg. Tranexamic acid 1 g is given intravenously within 3 hours of onset. Mechanical measures including bimanual compression, intrauterine balloon tamponade and, in refractory cases, uterine artery embolisation or B Lynch suture and hysterectomy are escalated in parallel. Well controlled essential hypertension is a relative but not absolute contraindication to ergometrine and requires blood pressure monitoring.
key_points: Escalation: oxytocin bolus and infusion, then ergometrine, then carboprost.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours of PPH onset.
Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, balloon tamponade) run in parallel to pharmacological escalation.
explanation.pearls: Atonic PPH after oxytocin: give ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscular next unless contraindicated, add tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours and prepare mechanical measures early.

subtopic_detail: Immediate antihypertensive choice for severe range blood pressure in pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 26 year old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents with a 2 day history of headache and epigastric pain. Her booking blood pressure was 108/64 mmHg. Today her blood pressure has been 166/112, 172/108 and 168/110 mmHg over the past 30 minutes on repeated automated cuff. Urinary protein creatinine ratio is 78 mg/mmol.

She has brisk reflexes but no clonus and no visual disturbance. Foetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. Bloods show platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L. She is on no regular medication and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 168/110 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Reflexes: Brisk, no clonus, no visual disturbance
data_table.Laboratory: Platelets 92 x10^9/L, alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (below 35), creatinine 78 micromol/L, urinary protein creatinine ratio 78 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive management?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and start magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading, then a 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis at this stage
options.rationale: In severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia, intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus (repeatable) plus magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis is a first line combination in AU. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Oral atenolol 50 mg once and observe for one hour to confirm response before adding any parenteral agent or magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention
options.rationale: Oral beta blocker with a slow onset is not appropriate for severe range blood pressure; magnesium sulfate should also not be delayed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure below 90 mmHg and hold magnesium sulfate until an eclamptic seizure occurs
options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate is not a first line agent in severe pre-eclampsia; magnesium is given for seizure prophylaxis with severe features, not only after a seizure. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg immediately for rapid onset and repeat every 15 minutes as needed to bring blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg within one hour
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine risks abrupt hypotension and foetal compromise; immediate release oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg is acceptable but sublingual dosing is not recommended. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg to reduce vascular volume and lower blood pressure and defer magnesium sulfate to prevent worsening of the pre-eclamptic profile
options.rationale: Furosemide is not indicated for severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia and worsens intravascular depletion; magnesium sulfate should not be deferred. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe range hypertension (systolic 160 mmHg or higher, or diastolic 110 mmHg or higher) in pre-eclampsia requires urgent antihypertensive therapy to prevent maternal stroke. In Australian practice the first line agents are intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus (doubling doses to 80 mg), hydralazine 5 to 10 mg intravenous, or immediate release oral nifedipine 10 to 20 mg (not sublingual). Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis when there are severe features, typically a 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion. Definitive management is delivery, with timing individualised by gestation, foetal wellbeing and maternal severity.
key_points: Severe range: systolic at or above 160 or diastolic at or above 110 mmHg needs urgent treatment.
Intravenous labetalol, hydralazine or immediate release nifedipine (not sublingual) are first line.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour infusion for seizure prophylaxis with severe features.
explanation.pearls: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks with sustained blood pressure over 160/110 mmHg: give intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus and magnesium sulfate 4 g loading followed by 1 g/hour infusion, and plan delivery.

sources.label: RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Statement
